result.report:
# Rust async runtimes: tokio vs thread-per-core designs

## Short answer

The evidence points the same way on the fundamentals: the mainstream option is production-proven and widely deployed [s1][s2], while the alternatives trade ecosystem breadth for simpler mental models [s3].

## What the sources agree on

- Work-stealing schedulers dominate real deployments; the primary documentation describes the multi-threaded runtime as the default [s1].
- Independent benchmarks show throughput within a few percent across runtimes for I/O-bound services [s2].
- Ecosystem compatibility, not raw speed, decides most migrations [s3][s4].

> "Choose the runtime your dependencies already chose." [s4]

## Where they disagree

One analysis reports a 30% latency advantage for the thread-per-core design under contention [s3], while the maintainers' own numbers show no measurable difference at p99 for typical request sizes [s1]. The disagreement comes down to workload shape, and neither source publishes its full harness.

| Criterion | Mainstream runtime | Thread-per-core | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scheduler | work-stealing [s1] | per-core queues [s3] | determines tail latency |
| Ecosystem | broadest [s2] | narrow | most crates assume the former |
| Learning curve | moderate | lower [s3] | fewer `Send` bounds |

## Practical guidance

```rust
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:8080").await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

Start with the default runtime unless profiling shows scheduler contention [s1][s2]. Re-evaluate when the thread-per-core designs stabilise their APIs [s3].
